intro: Twelve verses in which a man asks to be put on trial and then supplies the case against himself, on the assumption that it will not hold. It is worth reading with Psalm 17, which makes the same move; the two share the verb of the assayer refining metal. Grammatically this is the psalm of the first person singular perfect: I have walked, I have trusted, I have sat, I have hated, I have loved. Learn that ending here and you have half the narrative verbs in the book. Verse 8 is the one most people already know without knowing where it comes from, because it stands in the short prayer said on entering a synagogue.

stichs.en: Of David.
Judge me, LORD,
for I have walked in my integrity,
and I have trusted in the LORD; I will not slip.

verses.summary: The request is the opposite of what people usually pray for. He asks to be judged, not spared, and the reason he gives is not that he is good but that he has leaned somewhere.

stichs.en: Examine me, LORD, and put me to the test;
refine my kidneys and my heart.

verses.summary: Three verbs of inspection in a row, each with the object suffix. He is not asking to be looked at but to be taken apart.

stichs.en: For Your kindness is right in front of my eyes,
and I have gone about in Your truth.

verses.summary: The ground of the whole claim. What keeps him straight is not willpower but something he has kept in his line of sight.

stichs.en: I have not sat with men of emptiness,
and I will not go in among those who keep themselves hidden.

verses.summary: The evidence turns negative here and stays that way for two verses. What he offers the court is a list of rooms he has not been in.

stichs.en: I have hated the gathering of wrongdoers,
and I will not sit with the wicked.

verses.summary: The verb of sitting comes back from the verse before, and both times the company is a crowd. The vice being avoided is belonging, not any specific act.

stichs.en: I wash my palms in innocence,
and I go round Your altar, LORD,

verses.summary: The scene changes from the assembly of the wrong crowd to a rite performed alone. Washing and circling are both things done with the body before anything is said.

stichs.en: sounding out loud a voice of thanks,
and recounting all Your wonders.

verses.summary: Two infinitives that give the purpose of the circling. The point of the procession is that it is audible.

stichs.en: LORD, I love the dwelling of Your house,
the place where Your glory rests.

verses.summary: The centre of the psalm and the only line in it that states a positive attachment. Everything before was where he does not go; this is where he does.

stichs.en: Do not sweep my soul up with sinners,
nor my life with men of blood,

verses.summary: The one request in the whole psalm, and it is about company rather than safety. He asks not to be counted in the wrong tally.

stichs.en: in whose hands there is a scheme,
and whose right hand is full of bribes.

verses.summary: The men of blood get one verse of description, and it is about hands. The psalm has already spent verse 6 on what the speaker does with his.

stichs.en: But as for me, I will walk in my integrity;
redeem me and treat me with favour.

verses.summary: The opening claim comes back in the future tense, and immediately after it the speaker asks for a favour he has no way of earning. The two halves sit together without being reconciled.

stichs.en: My foot stands on level ground;
in the assemblies I will bless the LORD.

verses.summary: The verdict arrives without being announced: the man who said he would not slip is standing. And the crowd, which was the danger in verses 4 and 5, has become the place where he can speak.

pardes.body: The psalm is a ring. Verse 1 has him walking in his integrity and declaring that he will not slip; verse 11 has him walking in his integrity again and verse 12 has his foot standing on level ground. Everything inside that ring alternates between two kinds of company, the assembly of wrongdoers in verses 4, 5, 9 and 10, and the house where the glory rests in verses 6, 7 and 8. Read straight through, it is a man arguing that where you choose to stand is the same thing as who you are, and asking to be judged on that basis rather than on a list of deeds.

The word for integrity, {{1.5}} and {{11.1}}, is built on a root meaning whole or complete, not a root meaning clean; the claim is about being of one piece rather than about being without fault, which is why the same speaker can ask to be redeemed two words later without contradicting himself. {{2.3}} is the verb of the smith refining metal, and it also opens Psalm 17, where the same speaker says the refining has already been done. The pairing of {{2.4}} with {{2.5}}, kidneys and heart, is the standard biblical formula for what God examines in a person and it recurs in Jeremiah in exactly that role: the kidneys stand for the part of a decision that never surfaces in words.

The verb in {{9.1}} is the ordinary verb for gathering things in, and it is also the verb used when someone dies and is gathered to his people. That double sense is why the verse has been read both as a plea about the present, do not let me be swept up in the round-up when these people are caught, and as a plea about what comes after, do not file me with them at the end. The other question readers have always put to this psalm is how a person can say I have hated the assembly of wrongdoers and still stand at an altar; the common answer is to hear the whole speech as said before God rather than in front of witnesses, so that the boasting is testimony under examination rather than a public claim. Where that answer does not satisfy, the psalm is read as liturgy put in the mouth of anyone approaching the sanctuary, not as autobiography.

Verse 8 names two things and not one: the dwelling of a house and the place where the glory rests. In the mystical reading those are not synonyms; the house is the built structure and the glory is what consents to settle in it, and the whole point is that the second does not follow automatically from the first. The washing of {{6.0}} and the circling of {{6.3}} then describe a person making himself into the kind of vessel a presence would agree to occupy. The level ground of {{12.2}} is the same word used for what is straight and even, and it closes the psalm on the image of a plane with no tilt in it, which is what a thing has to be before something can rest on it without sliding off.
